title: Men’s Match Report: Lewes v Whitehawk - Lewes Football Club
content: Derby day delight for Lewes this weekend as they triumphed over local rivals Whitehawk. Report by Luke Hawkins It was an electric start from the Rooks who set the tone early on, with Tyler Cox latching onto a looping ball over the Whitehawk defensive line from Andrew Briggs. His touch took him beyond his man and allowed him to cut the ball back, leading to an early opportunity for Alfie Allen to test Hugo Fisher in the Whitehawk net, who saved well down to his right. There wasn’t much respite for the Whitehawk defence, as Lewes came at them again just minutes later. This time it was a low driven cross to the far post from Ryan Gondoh to find Noel Fisher, who couldn’t quite get the connection he desired. The one-sided nature of the first half continued when Gondoh thought he had provided the Rooks with the lead. The returning Rook was put through on goal by Noel Fisher but was ruled marginally offside. Another big chance fell the way of Alfie Allen, this time just before half time. The chance began with Andrew Briggs driving through midfield before playing into Calum Newson’s feet, who linked play well and rolled the ball over to the overlapping Allen who blasted just wide of the post. Craig Nelson’s team didn’t let the goalless half deter them, with the chances continuing to come thick and fast once play resumed, with the Rooks now facing the Philcox end. It was Calum Newson in behind this time, following a superb lofted pass from Andrew Briggs. Despite a well-timed run and a good touch to set himself, an excellent recovery run from Whitehawk’s Nikolai Krokhin saw Newson’s shot blocked. It didn’t take long for another big chance to arrive for Lewes who continued to dominate the game, with Jack Enkh firing just inches wide. His strike followed some excellent buildup play from the Rooks, who at this point, had the Whitehawk backline camped on the edge of the six-yard box. The visitors had a brief spell of threatening play, following the introduction of Victor Aiye. The second half substitute had Whitehawk’s best chance of the match when his flick from a corner sailed over the bar. Despite this positive period of play for the visitors, it was not a sign of things to come as Lewes resumed their relentless attacking play immediately after. The first of these chances fell to substitute Mackenzie Richardson, who headed wide after managing to win the resulting header from a botched Krokhin clearance. Just minutes later the Rooks were knocking on the door again, this time with Danny Bassett running through on goal following a perfectly weighted pass from Ryan Gondoh. Bassett did well to create the space between him and the recovering Krokhin but his shot on goal was ultimately a tame one, saved comfortably by Hugo Fisher. The Rooks resumed their attacking intent again, this time started by a commanding piece of defending by Tyrese Owen to win the ball back and start the move, with the ball being shifted out wide to Bobby Unwin off the bench. Unwin whipped in a dangerous cross which fell to Ryan Gondoh at the far post. He recycled the ball, and after a melee of shots into the crowded Whitehawk box, the ball was eventually cleared away. With just four minutes left on the clock, Lewes found themselves with a corner and potentially one of their last chances to claim victory in front of the 1889 in attendance, and that is exactly what they did. After a quick one two with Tyrese Owen, Ryan Gondoh crossed in a ball to the far post which was met emphatically by Mackenzie Richardson. The 18-year-old lost his marker and leaped highest to head home a dramatic winner in front of a packed Philcox stand. Seven minutes were added on but the Rooks marshalled the remaining time superbly, and after some excellent hold up from Danny Bassett earning a free kick by the corner flag, the final whistle was blown and the Dripping Pan could celebrate three incredibly hard-earned and deserved points. John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive (1972-2008), Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. “You got time to lean, you
got time to clean.” That’s what Roger, our manager at McDonald’s,
barked at us all the time. “That’s right, Time to Lean, Time to
Clean!” When we turned 16, my
identical twin brother Paul and I were hired at McDonald’s for $1.10
an hour. Back then, McDonald’s only employed male teenagers and
guys in their 20s. The only older people were the owner, Dick Lutz,
and our manager Roger, or as we all called him “Roger Dodger.” Both the owner and Roger
Dodger were cut from the Marine Corps side of life — crew cuts and
square jaws, no fooling around, though Rodger, had a twinkle in his
eye and a soft side. But the owner, Dick Lutz, always stomped around
like a caged bull. One time I said “Hello Mr. Lutz. Nice day.” He
stared at me like I was a buzzing mosquito. A bunch of our friends worked
at McDonald’s and we all jumped in with a gung-ho attitude to work
hard, make money and have fun. We wore those triangular cardboard
hats that made us look like carnival barkers but that was the price
we paid for a paycheck. We felt so jacked up about
working at McDonald’s that we competed at the front counter to see
who could book the most money during rush hours. The guys frying the
burgers were two-handed gun slingers, flipping rows of burgers,
laying them on buns and scraping the grill clean in seconds; true
greaseball performance artists. Without
doubt, the greatest burger gunslinger of all was Corky, the Hank
Aaron of the grill. We’d watch in amazement at Corky’s dexterity
as he flipped the burgers and laughed, a magician in a triangular
hat. For our lunch break we could
concoct any burger we dreamed up. We’d stack two or three patties
with cheese, chow down on a bag of fries and chocolate shake. Maybe
an apple pie, too. It sounds like the expressway to heart disease but
we were 16, so what did we care? We were all going to live forever
anyway. Our break room was located in
the basement, basically a shaky card table surrounded by towers of
burger boxes. In the corner stood a polished black safe and we
fantasized about sneaking in at 3 a.m. picking the lock and escaping
with a cool million dollars that we knew were stuffed inside that
safe. One day while clocking in and
I saw a thick red line drawn through my friend Corky’s name on the
employee list. The red line stretched across the page and ended with
a red skull and crossbones. I asked Roger Dodger, “What’s
the deal with the red line through Corky’s name?” “The owner saw him fooling
around last night and he doesn’t work here anymore.” I couldn’t
believe it. Corky, king of the grill, the hardest worker and
friendliest guy, gone? That’s so wrong. We investigated and found out
that the owner Dick Lutz had parked across the street one night and
spied on us with binoculars. He spotted Corky having some harmless
fun and that was enough for the owner to Red Skull him out of a job.
Gone like a hamburger wrapper in the wind. My friend Mike Huck said “I
bet he fired him because Corky was up to $1.85 an hour.” “Oh, come on. You don’t
think Mr. Lutz is that cheap, do you?” The next week, another guy
with seniority was fired. “They red-skulled Johnny
Landaal!” Mike Huck said. That day I walked downstairs
and sat with a couple of my co-workers. Mike Huck said, “I can’t
believe Dick Lutz can get away with treating us like that. That
sucks. Guess there’s nothing we can do about it.” I removed the bun from my
burger and peeled off the pickle and stared into space. Then I jumped
up and threw that pickle onto the sacred black safe, splattering
mustard and ketchup all over it. “If I ever find the guy who
threw that pickle on my safe, he’s fired!” and
signed it with a big red skull and cross bones. From that day, on my break,
I’d wait for the perfect moment and jump up and yell “Death to
the Red Skull” and slap my pickle on Dick Lutz’s shiny black
safe, mustard and ketchup flying and defiling that safe. Every single
day I worked. My blow against the empire, my pickle shot across the
bow. After that I morphed into a
very different worker than I’d been before. I’d be standing at the
counter and prop a handwritten note in front of me with an arrow
saying “Next window please.” One time I crawled on top on the
hamburger boxes and fell asleep in the middle of my shift. Or I’d
stand behind one of the counter guys and yell over his shoulder, “Can
I help you down here please?” and run back to my window I became so brazen in goofing
off that my lack of fear acted like a cloak of invisibility. For some
reason the owner and Roger Dodger never saw my craziness. My twin brother acted
completely the opposite of me. He always worked hard, didn’t pull
any stunts and kept to himself. He said to me one day, “Are you insane? Are you
trying to get fired? Mom and dad will be pissed. You’ve got to
stop.” I just told him, “The Red
Skull must be defeated,” One night a fellow worker came
in on his night off and ordered a small coke. My brother handed him a
large coke for the price of a small one, a difference of 5 cents.
Roger Dodger saw the exchange and said, “How much did you charge
for that large coke?” Roger called the worker up at
home and the guy lied for my brother and said he was charged 15
cents. So they fired my brother. I was outraged. I wrote a note. “I quit. You
can’t treat my twin brother that way,” and stormed out. “Look, If it was up to me,
I’d give your brother another chance but Mr. Lutz says we have high
standards at McDonald’s. Even if it’s only a nickel, that line
can’t be crossed.” Then he said, “Would you
please reconsider and still work for us? I think you are an excellent
counter guy.” I couldn’t believe it. How
could the world be so upside down? My brother, the perfect employee
and me, the pickle anarchist, and they’re begging me to keep
working? I said, “I don’t know,
Roger, that’s my twin brother you fired.” “I’m asking you to do it
for me, as a way to say I’m sorry. ” “Ok, Roger I’ll do it for
you.” I put my cardboard hat on and walked out to the counter. Roger yelled after me, “You
got time to lean, you got time to clean.” When I took my break, I ate my
double cheeseburger with my buddy Mike Huck and when I finished, I
started walking up the stairs. “What, no pickle on the safe
today? What’s going on? That’s the best thing that happens every
day. I look forward to it.” “No, I think it’s kind of
immature and I was getting tired of it. Plus, Roger was really nice
to me today.” But then, a week later Dick
Lutz drew a red skull through Mike Huck’s name and he disappeared,
too. That day I sat in the break
room with Jimmy, a french fry specialist. I said , “Jimmy, do you
think it will be like this at jobs when we grow up? “You know this whole “Time
to Lean, Time to Clean” crap and Red Skulling people, firing them
to save a few nickles ” Jimmy said, “Nah. I don’t
think so.” I think it’s just because we’re 16. It’s gotta be
different when we’re working as adults. Don’t you think?” “I don’t know, I don’t
know. But you wanna know what I really think, Jimmy?” “DEATH TO THE RED SKULL!!!”
I yelled as I slapped that pickle on Dick Lutz’ black safe one more
time, with gusto, ketchup and mustard flying everywhere, and I didn’t
feel one morsel of regret and I never would. « ‘Super’ El Niño is Projected to Bring Record-Breaking Rain to California, But Humboldt’s Forecast Is Less Certain. title: 3 winners and 2 losers from Heat’s preseason opener v. Raptors - Hot Hot Hoops
content: The final score doesn’t matter, but the Miami Heat took care of business in their first preseason game in Quebec City, Canada, against the Toronto Raptors this weekend. Nineteen players saw the floor for Miami, which is obviously a lot, especially since no starter played more than 14 minutes. So who were a few winners and losers? Let’s dive into it. Skinny: A concern for most of the offseason, the Heat’s 3-point shooting was their biggest strength on Saturday. In the first half on Saturday, 11 of the Heat’s 22 made baskets were from 3-point range, coming at a 47.8 percent (11-23) clip. Andrew Wiggins shot 4-of-6 from deep, while Tim Hardaway Jr. was a perfect 3-of-3. Miami did a great job pushing pace and exploiting an over-aggressive Raptors defense, both in the half-court and in transition. Obviously, it wasn’t perfect. It was a very physical game. Both teams were fairly disjointed, and that’s typically the case at this time of year. Miami’s 3-point shooting, however, wasn’t, and that’s a great sign to come if it can sustain even some of that. Skinny: Nothing that he showed tonight gives me concern about Conwell’s potential role as a rookie. Appearing 18 second-half minutes, he had six points on 3-of-8 shooting and two assists. For tonight’s game, he was on the outside-looking-in regarding the regular rotation, which isn’t far off from expectations to begin ths season. His defense was OK, and he missed all three of his 3-point tries. I’m not worried, but he didn’t pop in his first career NBA (preseason) action. Skinny: One point was painstakingly clear: As respected as Antetokounmpo is as a slasher and defender, his most underrated skill is his passing. He was phenomenal Saturday, dishing out a team-high seven assists — all coming on made threes. Giannis Antetokounmpo full highlights in his pre-season debut for the Miami Heat vs. the Toronto Raptors9 points on 3/3 FG, 3/4 FT, 4 Rebounds, 7 Assists (2 TOV), 1 PF, and a +/- of +4 in 14:07 minutes played.Like the other Heat starters, he played only the first half.I… pic.twitter.com/bdCN4umv7O He’s always been a good passer, a skill he’s tirelessly developed as he’s become a 1A superstar. He’s averaged 6.0 assists with a 32.8 assist rate over the last eight seasons, but it doesn’t get talked about as much because of how special of a slasher he is. And if his teammates are burying as many shots as they did tonight, he might set a new career high in those statistics. Here’s what Erik Spoelstra said about Antetokounmpo’s playmaking after the game. He makes great plays,” Spoelstra said, according to The Athletic’s Eric Nehm. “We knew that about him. We faced him in the playoffs three times. But when you really see it every day in practice this week, you appreciate how brilliant of a playmaker that he can be. “With the size and the vision and his ability to put it on the numbers to shooters is really impressive. Pat (Riley) was at practice all week and the way he’s played with the ball in his hands and delivering the ball, he reminds all of us of a great big point guard that played for Pat back in the ’80s.” Erik Spoelstra compared Giannis Antetokounmpo to Magic Johnson after the game tonight.Spoelstra: https://t.co/s7gWI3qJ2E pic.twitter.com/gRSZhDQidX Skinny: We will cut Thompson some slack: His gravity was evident, and he’s playing with an entirely new organization at 36-years-old. But he did not have a single point in 13 minutes, attempting two shots, including just one 3-pointer. To the point made in the first winner listed, Thompson being one of the few regulars to not make a three is an indictment of how good the rest of the supporting cast was from beyond the arc. Skinny: Of the Exhibit 10 signees, Schieffelin was the best one. The Heat decided to bring him in after an encouraging Summer League showing, and he picked up right where he left off. In 10 fourth-quarter minutes, he scored nine points on a perfect 4-of-4 shooting with one triple. Beyond that, his ballhandling and decision-making were crisp. He doesn’t move well nor does he have overwhelming athleticism, but the former two-sport athlete at Clemson has good coordination and knows how to impact the game without the ball in his hands. Of the Heat’s current Exhibit 10 players, he poses as the biggest threat to steal Vladimir Goldin’s two way, which — to me 0 — should be the most vulnerable. He was decent, which is an upgrade over last year awful. I m happy with that. Didn’t shoot well, but 7 rebounds and 4 assists were good. And one of his 2 blocks was on a great hustle play. Gotta get through East first. Heat bad news for East teams. Did you call AT&T yet? I would be surprised if they don’t have it. Did you try those channels I sent to you? title: Supreme Court set to hear Suncor v. Boulder climate lawsuit arguments - Key Biscayne Portal
content:
Mainly clear. Low 82F. Winds ESE at 10 to 15 mph.. (The Center Square) – A coalition of bipartisan lawmakers introduced legislation… (The Center Square) – The U.S. Food and Drug administration has proposed a rule … The U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. Photo: massmatt / Flickr / CC BY 2.0 / Cropped from Original (The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court is set to hear oral arguments Monday in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County. Supporters of Suncor and ExxonMobil argue there will be nationwide consequences as a result of this and dozens of other similar cases while some expressed confidence that the court will not allow one county to decide the energy policy of the nation. CEO of the American Energy Institute Jason Isaac told The Center Square that “the Supreme Court will hear the most consequential energy case of the term, and it isn't really about Suncor or ExxonMobil. “It's about whether a single county's jury can dictate energy policy for the entire country, a power the Constitution gives to Congress, not a courtroom in Boulder,” Isaac said. “The Justice Department itself has now told the Court as much, warning that one city cannot use its own state's law to set the rules for energy production nationwide,” Isaac said. “American Energy is confident the Court will side with the Constitution over courtroom lawfare, and with it, every American who fills a gas tank or pays a power bill,” Isaac said. Ongoing for years, Suncor Energy v. Boulder is essentially a lawsuit where Colorado’s Boulder County is attempting to make energy companies pay for the damages caused by climate change The Center Square reported it is “a case challenging whether state and local governments can utilize tort laws to seek billions in damages against energy companies over alleged contributions to climate change.” The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case in February 2026, with oral arguments set for Monday, Oct. 5. In August, 28 amicus briefs were filed in support of Boulder County, with a watchdog warning many of the briefs had connections to left-wing organizations and dark money. The briefs argue that the Supreme Court should allow the lawsuit brought by Boulder County go to trial. At a panel discussion hosted by the conservative Civitas Institute, University of Georgia law professor Hillel Levin said that federal law doesn't preclude state and local laws in cases such as this and it should go to trial. But president of the Judicial Crisis Network (JCN) Carrie Severino told The Center Square that Suncor v. Boulder “is a last resort for climate activists, who are attempting to hold energy companies accountable for past and future harm they say stems from global climate change.” “The case is part of a broader push by the left to weaponize the court and enact extreme environmental policies through lawfare, rather than through support from voters and lawmakers,” Severino said. Severino warned that “if Boulder succeeds, the floodgates could be open for states like Colorado and California to set national climate policy and regulate a number of industries in other states.” Executive director of consumer advocacy group Alliance for Consumers O.H. Skinner likewise told The Center Square that the lawsuit in question is a case of lawfare, or creating policies through the courtroom rather than the traditional legislative process. “Having lost at the ballot box, climate activists have turned to the courts to force through extreme policies that voters have rejected repeatedly,” Skinner said. “The Supreme Court’s ruling in Suncor will determine how far outside their borders a county or state may project their regulatory powers, and whether the nation’s energy policy is to be set by Congress or progressive activists in Boulder, Colorado,” Skinner said. As a point of interest, Severino told The Center Square how a “member of Boulder’s legal team admitted that their strategy is a bid to impose a ‘carbon tax’ that could bankrupt the energy industry and ultimately harm the American consumer.” “Beyond that, the sweeping claims at issue in Suncor could open the floodgates for similar lawfare-based litigation involving cars, firearms, and other sectors that are a huge part of everyday life,” Severino said. The Republic of Ireland’s Nations League clash with Israel will be played behind closed doors at a neutral venue as a result of growing unrest over the fixture. The two teams had been due to meet at Dublin’s Aviva Stadium on 4 October, but Uefa approved a request from the FAI in June to host the game overseas. The game will be held at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia, after Israel's ‘home’ match in Group B3 was played in Debrecen, Hungary last week. "Following consultation with various stakeholders, the Association is of the view that operational challenges could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil, so the fixture will be played away from the Aviva Stadium," the FAI said in a statement. "The Association thanks An Garda Síochana (Irish police) for their support and advice over recent months and states that the decision to relocate to a neutral venue is one that has been considered an appropriate course of action by the FAI Board with the support of Uefa." There had been growing calls within Ireland for the side to boycott the game amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The Republic of Ireland’s friendly against Qatar in May was disrupted after protestors threw tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag on to the pitch at the Aviva Stadium, while the Irish Sport For Palestine had launched a “Stop the Game” campaign. During last week’s game in Debrecen the Ireland players lowered their heads during the Israeli national anthem and sported black armbands to pay their respects to those who have lost their lives in Gaza. Irish captain Dara O’Shea approached the center of the field for the pre-match talk with his hands firmly clasped behind his back and did not shake the hand of Israel captain Manor Solomon, while Irish national broadcaster RTE opted for reduced coverage and reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazuno boycotted the match entirely, citing his “personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong.” Irish manager Heimir Hallgrimsson made clear his unhappiness over the fixture at his squad announcement, stating: “We are not playing with genocide, we are playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel, we are not playing with Israel.” Meanwhile the pre-match conference before Ireland’s home game was cut short after heated exchanges with members of the Israeli press. title: NFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Raiders, TV channels & live stream Sunday 4 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Chiefs and Raiders fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Disorienting as it may sound given the past 12 years of Chiefs-Raiders matchups, their game Sunday in Las Vegas is one of the blockbusters of the young NFL season. Kansas City have used Las Vegas (and before that, Oakland) as a doormat since the 2015 season, when Patrick Mahomes was a sophomore at Texas Tech. The Chiefs took both games from the Raiders that year and began a run of 18 wins in the teams’ last 22 contests, an unusual run of AFC West dominance in a league that adores parity. The Chiefs are favored again this week, but by less than a touchdown. The Silver and Black come in sporting a matching 3-0 record with their Missourian visitors. Kirk Cousins has found the fountain of youth at 38, keeping No 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza in an understudy’s role for at least a while longer. The 38-year-old has averaged at least 7.5 yards per pass attempt in each of the team’s three wins, two of which came on the road. The Raiders have benefited from a light opening schedule, taking advantage of games against the moribund Dolphins and Saints. Now comes a stiff test in the desert. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Football, or stream with NOW. Just how back is Patrick Mahomes? The answer might be “extremely.” The franchise QB was having the worst season of his career last year even before it ended a few weeks early because of a torn ACL. But now, Mahomes looks both accurate and unusually spry, like a man who’s gained mobility from chasing a bunch of little kids around his house. He is also benefiting massively from the arrival of Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker at running back. Walker is the league’s leading rusher, with 360 yards in his first three games with K.C. It’s not just volume, either; his 5.8 yards per touch are a career best. Cousins is getting the publicity, but the Raiders’ greatest strength to date is one that should come in extra handy against Mahomes: their sublime pass rush. Only one club, the Vikings, have generated more pressures than Vegas, according to Pro Football Reference. The biggest chunk of those (13) have come from the freakishly good Maxx Crosby, who only remains with the team because the Ravens backed out of a trade the teams had agreed to in March. It’s a team effort, though: Crosby only has two of the Raiders’ 10 sacks to date, a figure that places them tied for fourth. Mahomes will be minding his blind side.

title: Poetry Moment: 'to be the bird' by nicole v basta - WPSU
content: This is Poetry Moment on WPSU – a weekly program featuring the work of contemporary Pennsylvania poets. Your host is poet and author Marjorie Maddox, a 2023 Monson Arts Fellow, author of more than 20 books, and Professor Emerita of English and Creative Writing at the Lock Haven campus of Commonwealth University. Welcome to Poetry Moment. I’m Marjorie MaddoxWho hasn't, at some point, yearned to be a bird? In today's poem, "to be the bird," nicole v basta considers the storks of Poland, where, before moving to Pennsylvania, her ancestors lived, eventually working in the coal mines and garment factories of Wilkes-Barre. nicole v basta (who does not use capital letters in her name) is a 2026 Academy of American Poets Laureate Fellow. Her poems have appeared in Ploughshares, Blackbird, Third Coast, North American Review, and elsewhere. Her second chapbook, "the next field over" (2022), was published by Tolsun Books. nicole is also a community educator, arts events producer, and visual artist. Her work has been supported by grants and residencies, including Art Farm Nebraska, Monson Arts, and The Saltonstall Foundation. Currently, she is Poet Laureate of Tompkins County/Ithaca, New York. I'm told that, in Poland, storks migrate large distances to winter in Africa. After that long absence, their return is met with great anticipation. According to one source, "the sight of a stork circling overhead or tending to its massive nest is more than just a glimpse of nature; it’s a symbol of rebirth, good fortune, and deep cultural connection."... [S]torks restoring their nests. . . is a potent symbol [both] of renewal" and warmer days ("Storks: Poland's Beloved Harbingers of Spring"). In her poem, "to be the bird," nicole v basta also welcomes this majestic bird, embracing its "kind of solitude" as a gift. on the roof, a stork nests and dreams of a past lifewading in the shallow water of another continent beneath the roof, a woman goes on with her luckkneels to the narrow altar in the home she made of her body alone— suppose the silence after a quest-ion begins a new day, the quiet bouncing off the brims of hats— words like spar and spark, shoulder, the secondstar, limp in the air like lazy ghosts and suppose the answers arrive as the birds, not as the birthsthey've come to represent in the west, no, we're in the old country now and it is a gift, that kind of solitudethe one when there is no echo of yourself who breathes and what i am saying is— i may only wantto be the bird Originally published in Colorado Review Volume 50, Number 1, Spring 2023 Listen for Poetry Moment with Marjorie Maddox, Mondays during Morning Edition and All Things Considered on WPSU. You'll find more episodes at https://radio.wpsu.org/show/poetry-moment Have a tip for the WPSU newsroom? Email radionews@psu.edu.

title: Eddie Hearn says Dana White ‘completely cooked’ as Fury v Joshua promoter row rumbles on - Yahoo Sports
content: Eddie Hearn has said UFC boss Dana White is "completely cooked" as the row over who is involved with promotion of the upcoming Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua showdown continues to rumble on. Hearn and his Matchroom Boxing organisation promote Joshua, while Frank Warren represents Fury but White – backed by Saudi matchmaker Turki Alalshikh – and his Zuffa Boxing stable are adamant they will be involved in the production of the heavyweight fight for the Netflix broadcast. Hearn has been dead against this since the start and White wasn't at Wednesday's launch press conference for the blockbuster British bout, which he claimed was because of his obligation to attend UFC's Contender Series the day prior. White has insisted that he will be on the ground in Cardiff on 11 December for the fight itself but Hearn – who released a compilation video that went viral on social media this week of White giving a variety of confused and contradictory answers about the bout – has now hit out at his rival again in no uncertain terms. Gonna leave this one here 🫳 🎤 Time to move on to the big stuff. 10 weeks today the biggest fight in British boxing history! Let’s gooooo #FuryJoshua 🇬🇧 pic.twitter.com/tesKUojgPJ "To be honest with you, at this point, I think he's just completely cooked," Hearn said of the UFC supremo at a press conference in Birmingham following Ben Whittaker's victory over Conor Wallace on Saturday evening. "What he actually said was, 'We are doing the TV production,' which, again, in the contract is prohibited. "I wasn't going to drop that [compilation] video, by the way, because I thought, 'You know what? I'll leave it now.' I actually started to feel bad for him... "Then I woke up to [White's comments response] and thought I'll just drop the video. After that video, I spoke to SELA [Saudi events company], and I said, 'Have you seen his comments?' And they said, 'Yes, and it's completely untrue.' They told me that in writing. He cannot do that under the contract." Eddie Hearn is adamant that Dana White won't be involved with the fight (PA) On Saturday evening, White was at UFC 332, where Natalia Silva was crowned as the new UFC women's flyweight champion, and responded to Hearn's latest claims in typically defiant fashion. "I will be there," said White about his potential presence at the Fury-Joshua fight on 11 December. "We're producing the show. Just like Canelo [Alvarez vs Terence] Crawford [in September 2025], same thing. "Craig Borsari, Zach [Candito], my whole team – we will be producing the show. I will have my little phone on the table, just like tonight and every other night and every other show that I produce." Hearn did offer the slightest of olive branches to white, not only praising his tenacity but suggesting there will be a meeting in Los Angeles between the parties next week to iron out their differences and perhaps come to some sort of mutually agreeable conclusion. Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua came face to face at Wednesday's launch press conference (PA Wire) "I've gotta actually admire him," Hearn said of White. "Because rather than just going, 'Listen, fair play. Hearn's had me by the short and curlies.' Actually, there's not many of those, but he goes, 'No!' And he just won't give up. "So I've got to quite respect and admire it, because the front on him is unbelievable. But they want me to meet them in LA next week, which I probably will. "It could be to clear the air. It could be, 'What are we going to do? Are we going to keep doing this?' Ultimately, and I don't mean to sound arrogant, [White] cannot be involved in the fight unless myself and Anthony allow them to be. "They seem to be very desperate to be involved in the fight, and Turki [Alalshikh] wants them to be involved in the fight, and so do Netflix. And I get, like, it's great for the promotion. So I'm not against it – I just want you to tell me and explain why. Why should I? What's in it for Anthony? What's in it for us? And once we establish that, we can make a decision." Dana White insists no meeting with Hearn has been set up (AP) However, White promptly poured cold water on any suggestion of an amicable agreement by insisting that no such meeting has been set up. "I haven't heard anything about any meetings next week," White added. "Between who? What do I need to meet about? I answered this whole question. It's the same as it's been since however long we've been talking about this. "I hear nothing until you guys say it to me in press conferences. I don't care [who did the deal]. I'll be there. I'm producing it. I'm promoting it. I'll see you in Wales."

title: 4 Jaguars players fined for plays in Week 3 game v. Patriots - Yahoo Sports
content: Several Jacksonville Jaguars players were fined by the NFL for plays in last week's win over the New England Patriots. According to Ryan O'Halloran of the Florida Times-Union, these four Jaguars players received fines: S Antonio Johnson (roughness - penalty for punching at the football): $12,537 #Jaguars fines from New England gameTE Nate Boerkircher fined 8,625 for his low-block penaltyDE Arik Armstead $11,941 for facemask.C Robert Hainsey  $6,750 for low blockS Antonio Johnson $12,537 for roughness (penalty for punching at the football) Per the NFL rules and operations site, players receive a letter from the league informing them of what they did, along with a video of the play, why they are being fined, and how much it will cost them. "The NFL uses the fine schedule to outline the league's and the union's expectations for players to conduct themselves in a way that honors the sport and respects the game, themselves, their fellow players, the fans and the league. The rules are intended to protect the players from unnecessary risk, promote player safety and emphasize sportsmanship and respect of teammates, opponents, coaches, officials and fans." content: Dating rumours around BTS's V and Blackpink's Jennie are back in the spotlight. This time the spark is a passing remark in one of Jennie's recent interviews. title: CLÁSICO PREVIEW | Barcelona v Real Madrid - FC Barcelona Website
content: It's time for another Barça Femení Clásico at the Spotify Camp Nou (kick-off 7:00pm CEST). The league leaders are taking on their nearest rivals in a match that is always charged with plenty of emotion both on and off the pitch. The blaugranes come into it with an unblemished record of seven wins from seven so far this season – five in the domestic league and two in the Champions League. The all-whites have 13 points in the domestic league and two draws in Europe. Coach Pere Romeu gave his thoughts on the game in the pre-match press conference on Saturday. “​​The last game against Roma was one of the greatest games I have managed as a coach. It wasn't just a resounding victory, we played really well. This was really significant given what we had to deal with in September. We are also really developing as a team and I think that's worth mentioning. It will be a different and exciting Clásico, as they all are, and we will have to be at our best to come through the game”. The blaugrana coach also assessed their opponent's start to the season and style of play. “It's a different Real Madrid to last season. The team were a lot more direct last season, they played with more forwards, and this season they are playing with a midfield set up that is keeping the ball more, controlling possession. This means their attacking sequences are a bit longer than last season. It's a Real Madrid with new components and a slightly different style”. And he went on to discuss what might prove key in the match: “We have to keep the ball a lot, push hard after we lose it and try to limit the number of Real Madrid attacking transitions. We know they have other strengths, but one is fast play, counterattacks. If we manage that aspect properly, I'm sure we can come through in this game. This means we have to play a similar match to what we did in Rome, a lot of possession, hardly lose the ball, set the pace of the game. We have to avoid a basketball-type match, especially against a side like Real Madrid”. Pere Romeu has called up 20 players for the match: Gemma, Paredes, Van Asten, Sydney, Kerolin, Marta, Pina, Graham, Patri, Cata Coll, Aitana, C. Serrajordi, Pajor, Carla Julià, Brugts, Aïcha, Martina, McCamey, Rosalía and Mayssa. Today marks exactly six years since the first women's Clásico was played at the Valdebebas stadium. Barça ran out 0-4 winners, with Patri Guijarro scoring the first goal. Barça have managed to win 24 out of 25 of the games between both sides, which included the record setting match on 22 April 2022, when 91,648 were in attendance at the Spotify Camp Nou.

title: Cyrus Capital Partners v. Mexico: Investment Managers, Control and USMCA Legacy Investments - Aceris Law
content: On 30 July 2026, the arbitral tribunal in Cyrus Capital Partners, L.P. and Contrarian Capital Management, LLC v. United Mexican States rendered its Award in ICSID Case No. ARB/23/33, concluding that it lacked jurisdiction over the claims brought against Mexico under Chapter 11 of the North American Free Trade Agreement (“NAFTA”) and Annex 14-C of Chapter 14 of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (“USMCA”), which replaced the NAFTA following its termination.[1] The Tribunal was composed of Lord Collins of Mapesbury as President, David J.A. Cairns and Zachary Douglas KC, and the Award was dispatched to the Parties on 30 July 2026.[2] The dispute arose from debt securities (the “Notes”) issued by Mexican television company TV Azteca, S.A.B. de C.V. (“TV Azteca”) and, more specifically, from a September 2022 injunction issued by a Mexican court that allegedly prevented enforcement of the Notes and relieved TV Azteca from continuing to make payments on them.[3] Cyrus Capital Partners (“Cyrus”) and Contrarian Capital Management (“Contrarian”), together the “Claimants”, which acted as investment managers within fund structures that included the holders of the Notes, alleged that the Mexican courts’ treatment of their interests amounted to a denial of justice and breached the minimum standard of treatment under NAFTA Article 1105.[4] The Tribunal did not reach those substantive allegations, however, because it upheld two preliminary objections: first, that Cyrus and Contrarian were not themselves qualifying “investors” under NAFTA Articles 1116 and 1139, and second, that they did not possess a “legacy investment” within the meaning of Annex 14-C of the USMCA.[5] The Award is significant for investment managers and investment structures involving offshore funds because it draws a sharp distinction between managing an investment and owning or controlling it for treaty purposes.[6] It also provides an important interpretation of Annex 14-C of the USMCA, holding that an investment does not qualify as a legacy investment merely because the underlying asset was created while NAFTA was in force if the relevant investor only acquired it after NAFTA’s termination.[7] In August 2017, TV Azteca issued USD 400 million in 8.250% Senior Notes pursuant to an indenture, with the Notes scheduled to mature on 9 August 2024.[8] The Notes went into default in February 2021 and were accelerated by the trustee on 3 May 2022.[9] Cyrus itself did not hold the Notes, but acted as investment manager for Cyrus Opportunities Master Fund II, Ltd. (“Opps II Master”), a Cayman Islands company that was one of the relevant Noteholders.[10] Opps II Master acquired Notes with an aggregate principal amount of approximately USD 24.477 million through purchases made between late 2021 and November 2022, including purchases made after the September 2022 measure challenged in the arbitration.[11] Contrarian similarly acted through an investment structure in which Sandpiper Limited, a Cayman Islands company wholly owned by Contrarian Funds, L.L.C., was the registered owner of the relevant Notes.[12] Sandpiper acquired Notes with an aggregate principal amount of approximately USD 24.238 million from Contrarian Emerging Markets, L.P. on 13 March 2023, after the Notes had defaulted and been accelerated and after the alleged wrongful act had occurred.[13] The measure at the centre of the treaty claim was an injunction granted by a Mexican court on 27 September 2022 without a hearing or prior opportunity for the defendants to oppose the application, which allegedly relieved TV Azteca from continuing payments and prevented enforcement proceedings concerning the Notes in Mexico.[14] Cyrus and Contrarian maintained that, notwithstanding the fact that Cayman Islands entities were the registered Noteholders, their investment-management arrangements gave them control over those entities and the Notes and therefore entitled them to pursue claims as U.S. investors under NAFTA.[15] The Claimants filed their Request for Arbitration on 30 June 2023, one day before the expiry of the three-year period during which Annex 14-C preserved consent to arbitrate qualifying NAFTA legacy-investment claims.[16] Mexico raised a series of jurisdictional objections concerning, among other matters, the 90-day notice period under NAFTA Article 1119, the Claimants’ status as investors, the existence of a legacy investment under Annex 14-C, the timing of the alleged Article 1105 breach, Article 25 of the ICSID Convention, ratione temporis jurisdiction, NAFTA’s waiver requirement and Contrarian’s standing, as well as a separate admissibility objection.[17] The Tribunal ultimately needed to decide only two of those objections: whether Cyrus and Contrarian qualified as investors that had made, owned or controlled an investment under NAFTA Articles 1116 and 1139, and whether the Notes constituted legacy investments protected by Annex 14-C of the USMCA.[18] The first issue therefore turned substantially on whether the Claimants’ extensive contractual powers as investment managers amounted to “control” of the Notes for treaty purposes.[19] The second turned on whether Notes issued by TV Azteca in 2017 could qualify as legacy investments even though the entities through which the Claimants asserted their interests acquired the Notes only after NAFTA ceased to be in force.[20] The Tribunal held that Cyrus and Contrarian were not qualifying investors for purposes of NAFTA Articles 1116 and 1139 because they had not themselves made the relevant investment and did not own or control the Notes within the meaning of Article 1139.[21] The Tribunal separately held that the Claimants did not possess a “legacy investment” for purposes of Annex 14-C, because the relevant investment had to have been established or acquired by the claimant investor while NAFTA was in force, whereas the Claimants relied on the Notes’ original issuance by TV Azteca in 2017.[22] Because either conclusion was sufficient to defeat jurisdiction, the Tribunal declined to express any opinion on Mexico’s remaining jurisdictional and admissibility objections.[23] 1. Investment Management Was Not Equivalent to Treaty “Control” The Claimants argued that their investment-management agreements gave them broad authority over the Noteholders and their assets, including authority to make investment decisions, manage the Notes and exercise rights associated with the securities.[24] Mexico responded that the Cayman Islands funds, rather than Cyrus and Contrarian, owned the Notes and bore the corresponding economic interests, while the Claimants acted essentially as investment managers or agents.[25] After reviewing prior decisions including S.D. Myers, Inc. v. Government of Canada, International Thunderbird Gaming Corporation v. United Mexican States, B-Mex, LLC v. United Mexican States and Gramercy Funds Management LLC v. Peru, the Tribunal concluded that “control” under NAFTA Articles 1121 and 1139 was inextricably linked with ownership rather than mere management authority.[26] That distinction was decisive because Cyrus and Contrarian were not shareholders, co-owners or Noteholders but investment managers of corporate vehicles that ultimately included Cayman Islands companies holding the Notes.[27] The Tribunal acknowledged that the Claimants possessed broad contractual powers to purchase and sell investments and to exercise rights associated with them, but viewed those powers as consistent with the ordinary functions of an investment manager.[28] Crucially, the investment-management arrangements delegated powers to the Claimants without transferring the underlying ownership-level control, which remained with the relevant shareholders and corporate organs.[29] The Tribunal therefore found that the Claimants had no direct or indirect proprietary interest in the Notes themselves and could not claim the losses represented by amounts payable on securities legally held by separate entities.[30] The Claimants also relied on the economic interests of ultimate owners and general partners within their wider fund structures, including concepts of beneficial ownership under U.S. law.[31] The Tribunal rejected that approach, reasoning that it effectively disregarded the separate legal personalities deliberately used within the investment structures and that economic interests belonging to ultimate owners could not simply be attributed to the Claimants as investment managers.[32] This distinction also affected the character of the alleged loss because the sums due on the Notes were owed to the Noteholders rather than to Cyrus or Contrarian, while the Claimants had not framed their claim as one for lost investment-management fees.[33] Nor could Article 1117 cure the problem, since that provision concerns claims made on behalf of an enterprise of another NAFTA Party, whereas the relevant Noteholders were Cayman Islands companies and the Claimants had not brought an Article 1117 claim.[34] The result was therefore that extensive delegated management powers did not establish the ownership or control required by the particular NAFTA provisions on the facts and corporate structures before the Tribunal.[35] 2. A Legacy Investment Had to Be Established or Acquired by the Investor While NAFTA Was in Force Annex 14-C defines a “legacy investment” as an investment of an investor of another Party that was established or acquired during the relevant period while NAFTA was in force and remained in existence when the USMCA entered into force.[36] The Claimants argued that the temporal requirement was satisfied because TV Azteca had issued, and therefore “established”, the Notes in August 2017 while NAFTA was still in force.[37] Mexico, by contrast, argued that the words “established or acquired” referred to the manner in which the protected investor itself came to hold the investment, meaning that an investment acquired only after NAFTA’s termination could not obtain residual protection merely because the asset had existed previously.[38] The Tribunal accepted Mexico’s interpretation and considered that Annex 14-C simply distinguishes between an investor that itself “establishes” an investment and an investor that “acquires” an existing investment.[39] For the Tribunal, the textual requirement that the relevant asset be an “investment of an investor of another Party [to the treaty]” meant that TV Azteca’s issuance of the Notes in 2017 could not constitute establishment of the investment by Cyrus or Contrarian.[40] The separate requirement that the investment be “in existence” when the USMCA entered into force did not resolve the issue, as the Tribunal considered that language compatible with either interpretation.[41] The Tribunal also referred to Westmoreland Coal Company v. Canada (III), although it recognised that the issue in that case was different because Westmoreland concerned an investor that had disposed of its investment before the USMCA entered into force.[42] The Tribunal’s interpretation was further reinforced by the United States’ non-disputing Party submission and statements at the hearing that Annex 14-C required the claimant investor itself to have established or acquired the investment while NAFTA remained in force.[43] The Tribunal consequently held that the Claimants did not possess a legacy investment and upheld Mexico’s third jurisdictional objection.[44] An important limitation of the Award is that the Tribunal expressly declined to decide whether the purchase of distressed debt securities in the international market qualified as an “investment” for treaty purposes.[45] The Tribunal likewise did not decide Mexico’s objection that NAFTA Article 1105 could not be breached by conduct occurring after NAFTA’s termination, an issue that has featured in other disputes arising from the transition between NAFTA and the USMCA.[46] It also left unresolved Mexico’s objections concerning the 90-day notice period, Article 25 of the ICSID Convention, acquisition of some Notes after the alleged denial of justice, compliance with the NAFTA waiver requirement, Contrarian’s standing and admissibility.[47] The Award should therefore be read principally as a decision on investor identity and control and on the temporal definition of a legacy investment, rather than as a comprehensive interpretation of all jurisdictional questions arising under Annex 14-C.[48] Having determined that it lacked jurisdiction, the Tribunal applied the principle that the unsuccessful party should bear the successful party’s costs and found no reason to depart from it in the circumstances.[49] The total costs of the arbitration amounted to USD 457,803.09, and the Tribunal ordered the Claimants to reimburse Mexico USD 301,519.69 in respect of arbitration costs, as the difference between the total costs of the arbitration and the amounts advanced by the Claimants, and USD 462,050.89 for Mexico’s legal fees and expenses.[50] Those amounts were ordered to bear simple interest from the dates due until payment at the 30-day SOFR rate plus 2%.[51] The Cyrus Capital Partners v. Mexico Award illustrates that, in complex fund structures, the entity exercising day-to-day investment authority is not necessarily the entity that owns or controls the investment for purposes of investment-treaty jurisdiction.[52] Broad contractual powers to select investments, exercise securities rights and direct investment strategy may constitute management authority without transferring the ownership-level control required by the applicable treaty.[53] The Award also demonstrates the jurisdictional importance of respecting the separate legal personalities within investment-fund structures, since economic interests belonging to ultimate owners cannot automatically be attributed to an investment manager further down or alongside the corporate chain.[54] With respect to the NAFTA-USMCA transition, the Tribunal adopted a claimant-specific interpretation of Annex 14-C: it is insufficient that an underlying asset happened to exist while NAFTA was in force, because the investment must have been established or acquired by the protected investor during the relevant period.[55] At the same time, the Award leaves several broader questions concerning NAFTA legacy claims unanswered, including whether Annex 14-C permits claims based on post-termination breaches of NAFTA obligations and how distressed debt should be treated as an investment under NAFTA and the ICSID Convention.[56] [1] Cyrus Capital Partners, L.P. and Contrarian Capital Management, LLC v. United Mexican States, ICSID Case No. ARB/23/33, Award, 30 July 2026, paras. 1, 163, 264. Europe | Middle East | Africa | Asia | Oceania | North America | South America

title: Suncor v. Boulder Brings Future of State Climate Litigation Before Supreme Court - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. The U.S. Supreme Court begins its new term by reviewing a closely watched climate litigation case. On October 5, the Court will hear arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County on whether communities or states may use state tort law to hold energy companies liable for alleged harms associated with global climate change. Boulder is one of roughly two dozen municipalities, along with nine states, that are seeking billions of dollars from oil companies for alleged climate-related harms. In Boulder’s case, the county filed a lawsuit in 2018 using public nuisance laws to redress in-state harms from deceptive marketing practices and upstream production activities. Boulder contends that Suncor and ExxonMobil deceived the public about the role of fossil fuels in climate change and are responsible for damages incurred by local authorities to mitigate harm to the community. Suncor and the other defendants failed to have the case removed to federal court, arguing that interstate and international greenhouse gas emissions fall under federal authority. They filed a motion to dismiss with the state district court, which was also denied. The Colorado Supreme Court reviewed the question of whether federal law preempts Boulder’s state-law claims and ruled in May 2025 that the case should proceed under Colorado law. In August 2025, Suncor and Exxon asked the Supreme Court to consider the case; their petition was granted in February 2026. The U.S. Supreme Court has outlined two questions for the litigants to address on October 8. In addition to the merits question concerning preemption, the Court has raised a threshold question of timing: whether it has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear the case. Boulder argues that the Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction to review the case at this stage. They contend that the companies “merely asked the state court to review the district court’s ruling and, ultimately, reverse it.” In the Brief for Respondents, Boulder states that no final judgment was entered and that the petitioners were impatient, running “to this Court at the case’s outset” rather than letting “the state judicial process play out.” Suncor and Exxon insist that the state court process has in fact played out, that the Colorado Supreme Court acted “as a court of first resort, rather than an appeals court” when it ruled the state-law tort claims were not federally preempted. If the Court accepts jurisdiction and moves to the merits of the case, the Court’s decision could have significant implications for the federal preemption question in similar climate-change lawsuits. Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County v. Suncor Energy (U.S.A.), Inc. was just the second state climate lawsuit to survive an appeal to a state’s highest court. Boulder argues its claims do not infringe on federal authority because it seeks damages for deceptive marketing practices that allegedly harmed the community, rather than the abatement or regulation of emissions. It therefore contends that the claims should proceed under state tort law rather than federal common law. In City of New York v. Chevron Corp., the Second Circuit dismissed a similar argument about the absence of a demand for regulatory relief, remarking that these climate-change lawsuits are beyond the limits of state law. The real goal of New York City’s lawsuit, according to the court, was “to effectively impose strict liability for the damages caused by fossil fuel emissions no matter where in the world those emissions were released (or who released them).” Earlier this year, the Maryland Supreme Court offered a similar warning as it dismissed three climate-change lawsuits. Justice Brynja Booth wrote: “No amount of creative pleading can masquerade the fact that the local governments are attempting to utilize state law to regulate global conduct that is purportedly causing global harm.” Lawsuits from Boulder and Honolulu have been cleared by each state’s high court to proceed to trial. Cases from New York City and three Maryland communities have been dismissed by those states’ high courts. Many expect that the Supreme Court’s decision will clarify the federal preemption question in relation to climate change litigation. The fact that almost 70 merits-stage amicus briefs were accepted by the Court illustrates the high stakes of next week’s hearing. Members of Congress take opposing positions on whether Boulder is impermissibly applying Colorado law extraterritorially. A group of 90 Democrats and Independents argue that Boulder seeks to apply Colorado tort law to obtain restitution for damages allegedly caused by the defendants’ deceptive marketing practices. They contend that the lawsuit does not seek to regulate emissions outside of the state and therefore does not intrude on federal authority. An amicus brief of 74 Republican Members of Congress states that the Colorado decision “would allow a patchwork of conflicting state laws around the country to govern matters of uniquely federal concern.” The Constitution grants Congress and the President the power to set energy policy, enact environmental standards, and direct foreign policy. Former Attorney General William Barr claims that a fundamental defect in Boulder’s case is that it intrudes on foreign policy. He warns that a “state liability regime that imposes its own costs on American companies for global emissions would necessarily alter that national balance.” Suncor claims that Boulder’s lawsuit is an attempt to set not only foreign policy but economic policy as well. Suncor and several supporting amici argue that allowing state courts to assign liability and damages for global emissions would effectively permit states to set national energy and climate policy. Boulder maintains that state courts may impose liability for local harms allegedly caused by the defendants’ conduct, even though the alleged climate-related effects involve global fossil-fuel production and emissions. A brief from the Natural Resources Defense Council supports Boulder’s position, arguing that climate attribution science has advanced to the point that scientists can quantify fossil fuel producers’ “contributions to specific extreme weather events.” A brief from climate economists disputes concerns that making energy producers pay damages would destabilize the American economy. They assert that insulating these companies from bearing the social cost of carbon is a market inefficiency that needs correction. Last year, David Bookbinder, who previously represented Boulder in the case, described the lawsuit as “a somewhat convoluted way to achieve the goals of a carbon tax,” explaining that “the people who use the products pay for the damage that they cause.” He also said that if state courts imposed liability for the costs of global climate change, the immediate result would be every fossil-fuel producer declaring bankruptcy. Courts in California, New Jersey, and Delaware have halted state climate litigation pending the Supreme Court’s decision. At present, Honolulu v. Sunoco is proceeding with discovery in Hawaii state court. Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from the case without explanation. A 4-4 split would leave the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision in place without establishing a controlling Supreme Court precedent on the preemption question. title: Munster v Bulls: Five takeaways as 'rookie inclusion' becomes '16-point game-winning masterstroke' - Planet Rugby
content: Ex-Ireland U20s out-half Charlie O'Shea starred for Munster as did Jeandre Rudolph, inset, for the Bulls Following a 26-22 win for Munster against the Bulls in their URC clash at Thomond Park on Saturday, Planet Rugby picks out five takeaways from the round two action. What a timely success for Munster following a difficult start to the new season that featured an opening round defeat, plenty of injury concerns and the resignation of the club CEO. After an eventful week, it all came right on the night and the riposte had a headline maker in 20-year-old rookie Charlie O’Shea. Making his first start, he scored 16 points – two tries and three conversions – and produced the assist for another, a wonderful 70-minute contribution that came out of the blue given his team’s inconsistencies and a low level of expectancy surrounding them. Buoyed by their sharp start to the season at Zebre, the Bulls were first to strike in this fixture, pouncing off a 15th minute maul through Ruan Vermaak, but that opener was soon matched by O’Shea’s precision 19th minute cross-kick to the unmarked Diarmuid Kilgallen. This reply energised the hosts and with the home crowd roaring its approval, they took the lead in the 31st minute when O’Shea charged down a Curwin Bosch kick and won the race versus Zak Burger to the ball that had bobbled over the try line. The advantage didn’t linger, as Thaakir Abrahams’ break scrambled the defence and Francois Klopper provided the 36th-minute pick-and-drive converted try finish for 14-all. It was another Jeandre Rudolph penalty-winning breakdown intervention that allowed Bosch to kick the South Africans into a 44th-minute lead, but this swing didn’t demotivate Munster. O’Shea’s second try on 55 minutes, following a carry to the line by John Hodnett, got them back into a lead that was added to by Alex Kendellen’s follow-up 14 minutes later. Up 26-17, the finish became a tense situation with Rudolph’s 73rd-minute try cutting the margin to four points, but Munster deservedly held on. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Munster boss Clayton McMillan made wholesale changes following last weekend’s opening round loss and the inclusion of O’Shea, the first-year academy out-half, for his first start proved a masterstroke. The 20-year-old had debuted off the bench in the final minutes of the collective fade-out against Glasgow, but the rookie’s impact was beyond anyone’s wildest dreams. He settled encouragingly to the task, and his grabbing of a clearance kick over the touchline and keeping it in play was a sign of his early composure, and what followed was immense. His bomb of a cross-kick on penalty advantage created Kilgallen’s score. Then came his own two tries. The first was a splendid piece of opportunism, charging down the Bulls kicker and then winning the race to dive on the ball over the line. And the second was well-timed. Munster mistakes had allowed the Bulls several escapes, but O’Shea punished them in the corner 15 minutes in the second half with a lovely shuffle and dive. He continued to lead by example, executing a splendid 61st-minute touch finder, and his final act was the conversion of Kendellen’s try, which was followed by a standing ovation as he made his way off. After all the concern about inadequate cover for the injured Jack Crowley, a new hero had unexpectedly been found. Glasgow v Ulster: Five takeaways as second-half ‘card thriller’ ends with ‘Springbok hopeful’ securing a draw The Bulls swaggered into the new season in the nice surroundings of balmy Italy last weekend, but an autumnal Ireland proved not to be to their liking as they failed to reach the pitch in the performance that was needed to see off their enthusiastic hosts. It was just four months ago when the South Africans hammered Munster 45-14 on the Highveld in the quarter-finals, but that polish was absent at Thomond Park on a night where the Bulls never seemed happy with the conditions. They gave up nine penalties to Munster’s five, including one at a first-half scrum, an area of the game that is usually their forte, and their level of turnovers was just too much. They had a class act in No.8 Rudolph, but the defensively shaky manner in which they conceded the first two tries – a cross-kick and a charged-down kick – highlighted that the reaction time of too many players wasn’t good enough. It said a lot that despite having six minutes to rescue themselves after cutting the deficit to four points, no good chance followed to snatch a victory from the jaws of defeat. Sharks v Leinster: Five takeaways as Springboks stars ‘at the forefront’ of hosts’ onslaught in memorable win over champions There is nothing like a good head-to-head duel, and the clash of the respective No.8s was a decent watch. For some time, Brian Gleeson has been spoken about as the next great thing in the Munster pack, but injuries have blighted the fulfilment of this fine promise. Until now, perhaps. With his body now more seemingly accustomed to the bangs and knocks of the pro ranks, the 22-year-old was a prime reason why Munster got their win. When it came to bally carrying, there was no teammate to match his frequency of industry, and it was a pity that he needed to go off for a HIA after a 65th-minute collision. Whereas Gleeson certainly has youth on his side to forge what it is hoped will be a distinguished career, it’s a different situation for the 32-year-old Rudolph. Currie Cup has long been his playground, but last year’s switch to the Bulls has provided the platform for him to shine on an elevated stage. He is a different type of player to Gleeson – it’s Marcell Coetzee who remains the Bulls’ go-to for ball carrying. But Rudolph was incredibly difficult for Munster to shift when he latched onto their breakdown ball, and he exhibited an impressive show of pace with the touchline dash he made for his try near the end. Six-try Dragons claim bragging rights over Scarlets in high-scoring Welsh derby Munster’s attack got some flowers before fading last weekend, but this was another step forward as regards basic execution. The score was 19-17 in their favour when they packed down for a scrum in the middle of the pitch on the 22, and what followed was the sort of threat they have generally lacked for quite a while. The impressive Craig Casey found Dan Kelly, another who played well, with a long pass and the midfielder’s immediate transfer got rookie Gordon Wood to a ruck about seven metres out where the presentation was crisp, allowing Casey to hit the support line running Kendellen to score. That was excellent, no-nonsense play. Not so good, however, was Munster’s worsening injury profile with Michael Milne and try-scorer Kilgallen early departures. It didn’t help either having to select an ex-England prop as their back-up hooker. They got just over an hour from the debut-making South African Marnus van der Merwe, but what followed at the lineout with Kieran Brookes on the throw was an example that cover can only stretch so far. Better teams than the Bulls would have made Munster pay. title: Michigan v Minnesota recap, results: Gophers beat Wolverines at home for the first time since 1977 - Yahoo Sports
content: The Little Brown Jug is staying in Minneapolis after Minnesota beat Michigan at home for the first time in nearly 50 years. The Golden Gophers (4-1) held the Wolverines (3-2) scoreless in the second half of a 20-14 victory Saturday. It's Minnesota's first home victory over Michigan since 1977, an 18-game streak that ended with Gophers fans storming the field. "This team's heart, their how, their spirit," Minnesota coach PJ Fleck said. "Our community and state, they never stop believing in anything. This team is resilient. There's pandemonium in Minneapolis right now." Michigan held a 14-7 lead at halftime but had the ball for only 47 seconds in the third quarter because of three consecutive turnovers, the first on a muffed punt by Andrew Marsh and then an interceptions by quarterback Bryce Underwood. Michigan started the fourth quarter on another interception by Underwood, who completed 10 of 21 passes for 101 yards and a QB rating of 69. Minnesota took the lead for good on a 3-yard TD reception by Darius Taylor from Drake Lindsey, who completed 17 of 25 passes for 136 yards. Minnesota's most recent win in the series that awards The Little Brown Jug was 12 years ago in Ann Arbor. "Besides my marriage, my kids being born, this might be the best day in my life," Fleck said.

title: 2026 Lions v Panthers: Friendly Rivalries Set Tone For Sunday Night’s Game - Yahoo Sports
content: A friendly family rivalry gives Lions' OC Drew Petzing one more reason to eagerly anticipate Sunday night's contest against the Carolina Panthers. His younger brother, Dean Petzing, is an offensive quality control assistant with Carolina. This game marks the third consecutive season the brothers have squared off on opposite sides of the field. The record currently stands at 1-1, and Sunday's game represents the tiebreaker, with the winner taking home the highly coveted annual bragging rights.At Thursday's media session, Drew Petzing went on record saying, "Obviously, I love him, and he's very close to me. But on Sunday, I hope he has a really bad game." Talking about how the brotherly rivalry developed over the years, Petzing explained, "I've gone against him a lot, video games, et cetera…I think it's probably more stressful on my parents than it is on us. We just want to win. I think he probably wants us to lose by 50, and I want him to lose by 50. I don't think that's ever going to change. Our parents are going to be stressed out and probably want just a really high-scoring game on both accounts, and a tie game if that could ever happen. But it's fun. I talk to him. I wouldn't say it's any different. I really don't treat it any different." As much as he enjoys the friendly rivalry, Petzing admitted having a close relative in a similar position who understands the challenges of playing in the NFL who he can share things, is a tremendous advantage: "Absolutely. It's someone that when I talk to him, it's fun to be able to talk football, and talk the job, and talk different things you're seeing around the League. And we both grew up huge fans of the sport. So, it's something that has been in our lives and been in our family since as early as I can remember." Although Petzing is new to the Lions this season, he is already making a positive impact with the 2-1 Lions' offense, consistently scoring 31 points per game. Petzing is developing a strong connection with his MVP-caliber quarterback, Jared Goff, leveraging Goff's precision passing skills while encouraging him to be more mobile. On Sunday night, Goff is likely to surpass his childhood idol Joe Montana on the NFL's all-time passing yards list. Needing only 128 yards to reach that mark, Goff has already set one league benchmark this season. He enters Week 4 with a Top 3 passer rating of 116.1 and is the only NFL quarterback to have thrown for more than 8 touchdowns with zero interceptions. As a play caller, Petzing has shown an affinity for spreading the ball around and keeping defenses off balance. Detroit's stellar ground game has flourished this season, with Jahmyr Gibbs recording 65 carries for 307 yards, four touchdowns, plus another two scores on 18 receptions for 156 yards. Petzing further endeared himself to the Detroit fan base when he was spotted playing with his young daughter, Emilia, on the field ahead of the Week 1 game against the New Orleans Saints. Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing hands his daughter Emilia a football ahead of a game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. While much has been made of the 1-1 Petzing brothers' connection, they are not the only coaches or players with strong ties to the Carolina area. Detroit assistant head coach and wide receivers coach Scottie Montgomery is a native of Shelby, North Carolina. He played wide receiver at Duke, where his record of 171 career receptions still stands as the university's second-highest. After playing for the Panthers as a rookie in 2000, Montgomery spent time with the Denver Broncos and Oakland Raiders before turning his attention to coaching. He became the wide receivers coach at Duke in 2006 and the head coach at East Carolina in 2016 before joining Dan Campbell in Detroit in 2023. Detroit Lions assistant head coach and wide receivers coach Scottie Montgomery looks on during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 17, 2026. In addition to the family and friends at Bank of America Stadium cheering on behalf of Petzing and Montgomery, three Lions' players also have strong Carolina connections. Center Cade Mays, who was drafted by the Panthers in 2022 in the sixth round and spent the last four years with Carolina, helped the team earn their first division title in 10 years in 2025. Although Mays is currently on IR recovering from a fractured wrist, his free-agent signing by Brad Holmes this past March looks like a grade-A move for Detroit. Lions' free agent EDGE D.J. Wonnum attended college in South Carolina and played for the Panthers in 2024- 2025 after being drafted by the Minnesota Vikings in the 4th round of the 2020 NFL Draft. Now in his first season with Detroit, Wonnum has become the perfect complement to Aidan Hutchinson. While the pair present a two-headed threat for the opposition, Wonnum has racked up seven tackles (four solo), 2.0 sacks, a pass defense, and a fumble recovery in three games. Like Mays, Holmes' free agent acquisition of Wonnum has been an undeniable success and is continuing to pay big dividends for the team. Finally, DL Alim McNeill, a native of Raleigh, North Carolina, who was drafted by the Lions as a third-round pick in the 2021 NFL Draft out of N.C. State has returned to his elite form this season. McNeill has been on an absolute tear this season following a disappointing injury-shortened 2025. His five tackles (four solo) and 2.0 sacks don't adequately reflect McNeill's disruptive impact when he is on the field, seemingly everywhere all at once, causing chaos. Sep 27, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions defensive line Alim McNeill (54) tackles New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) during the first quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images On the other side of the field, Carolina punter Sam Martin previously played for the Lions from 2013 through 2019. Martin was the Lions' fifth-round draft pick in 2013. The Lions have a great deal riding on this game. The Vikings are currently atop the NCF North division at 3-0. Detroit is tied with the Bears at 2-1. A win in Carolina on Sunday night will potentially determine the narrative for this season; are the Lions a contender or merely a pretender? The friendly rivalries are an added incentive that could set the tone for this game. One thing is certain for Detroit: despite the Lions playing on the road Sunday night, with so many Lions' coaches and players having strong Carolina connections, this game will be a homecoming of sorts with a huge contingent of family and friends at Bank of America Stadium cheering Detroit on to victory. title: Fiery as ever, Hilton's Lipani sets Section V football wins record - Democrat and Chronicle
content: Rich Lipani spent much of the last week downplaying the significance of Section V's all-time wins record, referring to the chase as a function of his experience. That chase is now over. Hilton's longtime head coach, still fiery as ever, stands alone atop the area's record books. No. 231, a dominant 56-19 victory for the Cadets over Webster Schroeder, pushed Lipani past Dave Whitcomb, who held the record for the last couple years. "It's fantastic. A lot of the guys I've coached over the years that aren't with the team anymore were back tonight to help celebrate a little bit," Lipani said. "It's a great night overall, but we'll move on to next week and see what happens." Lipani nabbed win No. 1 some 40 years ago as head coach at Greece Arcadia. The former three-sport star at Greece Athena had recently finished his playing career at SUNY Brockport, and in 1986 took over a Titans program with little football tradition. Within two years, Arcadia won its first (and only) Section V football title. Following a three-year stint Lipani relocated slightly west to Hilton, where he was already a physical education teacher. In 1988, the year before Lipani was hired, the Cadets endured a winless season. And within a few years, again, Lipani turned that team into a championship winner. Now the four-time section title-winning head coach is to Section V what Don Shula is to professionals. Beyond the win total, Hilton assistant coach Andy Forman — who played under Lipani at Arcadia — thinks his head coach's longevity deserves recognition. A coach that sticks around for 40 years is a rare one indeed. "Nobody coaches that long anymore. He's a special guy to be able to do it. He's been able to adapt and overcome," Forman said. "His big message is that he wants football to be the best time of the kids' life when they're here at Hilton. That's what he really strives for." Forman acknowledges Lipani's sideline intensity, another trait from a bygone era, but said the coach's impassioned demeanor doesn't tell the entire story. "He's the most intense guy I've ever seen. We weren't much of a football school at Arcadia before he came, but his intensity was contagious right away. He brings it now the same way he did in '86," Forman said. "But he's one of the funniest guys you'll ever meet. You might not think that when you see him on the sidelines, but he's the best." There was little to laugh about on the opening play of Friday's game, when Schroeder's Sam Hilfiker took the opening kickoff about 70 yards to the doorstep of the end zone. Schroeder took the lead on the next play, only 13 seconds into the game. It was an unfamiliar position for the perfect Cadets, but not long-lasting. On Hilton's first offensive play from scrimmage, senior Tyler Reger dashed left for a 74-yard score. The first play of the Cadets' second possession, Reger again attacked the left sideline for an 83-yard touchdown run. By game's end, Reger had nearly upstaged his coach's historic night. His seven touchdowns were one short of the Section V record, held by a handful of ex-players. "(The opening kickoff) made us have to do something we haven't had to yet. We had to bounce back, with our backs against the wall a little bit there. That was a big drive for us after. That's what we've been preaching all year, because that's what it's gonna take down the road." Unbeaten and averaging about 48 points through five weeks, Hilton shows no signs of slowing down. Neither does its coach. Asked how long he wants to continue in his role in a recent appearance on the Varsity Voices video podcast, Lipani offered no expiration date. “If they want me back and I feel I’m doing a good job, I’ll come back for another year. If I think I’m not doing a good job, I’ll step away,” Lipani said. “Just doing the best I can every day. The guys I’ve got working with me are doing a great job and we all enjoy it. One day at a time, one year at a time.” Totals accumulated by the New York State Sportswriters Association Our editors independently choose our recommendations.
