title: Republic of Ireland news conference ends abruptly amid accusations - BBC
content: The Republic of Ireland's news conference before their second match against Israel ended abruptly as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists. One reporter tried to ask Hallgrimsson for his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers overpowered the attacker and successfully took control of the plane. The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist, who refused to give up the microphone, about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary. The news conference was brought to a close at that point by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) communications manager Kieran Crowley, who said those allegations were "completely untrue" as the mood soured. Allegations of racism by Irish players follow on from the FAI announcing it is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans during the first match in Debrecen, which Hallgrimsson's team won 3-0. At Israel's news conference later in the day, the team's media officer stepped in to confirm the Israel FA has not lodged a complaint with Uefa but "will think about that after the match tomorrow". "Our players told us there was trash talk between the Irish players and them that was not like normal or like any other match," the media officer said. Head coach Ran Ben-Shimon did not want to address such matters, insisting "a good result tomorrow is my only focus". Before the Irish news conference was cut short, Hallgrimsson said similar as he stressed he would not "get involved in that as others will process that". "It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said. "I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa. "Something was reported by both teams, so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this. "I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about." Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Hallgrimsson's side face Israel in Serbia on Sunday after their 3-0 win over the same opposition last week This has been a challenging international window for the Republic of Ireland, with the Israel fixtures dominating discourse in Irish football. Since the teams were drawn together in February, a 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine, which called for a boycott of the fixtures in protest against the ongoing Israel-Gaza war. Before last week's 'home' game for Israel in Hungary, Republic of Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the fixtures, saying "it would be wrong to participate", while a vote by players to play the games passed by a "significant majority", according to FAI chief executive David Courell. The players wore black armbands during the game "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict". The Republic of Ireland then played Austria in Dublin on Thursday, when protests resulted in tennis balls being thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag. Hallgrimsson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged". They have four points from three games so far, having beaten Israel and drawn 2-2 with Austria. They lost 1-0 to Kosovo in the campaign opener. "The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other," Hallgrimsson said. "Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is. "When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals." The Republic of Ireland boss revealed the team have taken part in a group prayer before leaving the dressing room for recent games, which he said was "just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch". He said that has been led by midfielder Conor Coventry whom he joked is now known within the squad as "Brother Coventry". The Icelander said Dara O'Shea - the team's captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off. title: CBS News poll finds voters split on state v. national focus in tied Maine Senate race - CBS News
content:
Updated on:  October 2, 2026 / 10:10 PM EDT
            / CBS News Anyone who's walked its rugged coast or skied in its mountains knows Maine can get windy.But right now Maine's Senate race seems a bit insulated from the national political winds — which otherwise seem to favor the Democrats — at least enough to keep incumbent Republican Susan Collins in a tied race with Democrat Troy Jackson in a state that otherwise has a Democratic-leaning electorate. Collins is drawing enough voters and enough of Maine's Democrats, while she is bolstered by those who say they're voting more on state matters than national ones, to keep the race at a tie. And she has an edge on who would bring back more federal funds to Maine. Jackson's challenge is that Collins peels off one in five voters who disapprove of Trump — a rate higher than what Republican congressional candidates get nationally. Jackson's backing, in turn, is driven by those who think Collins is too much in agreement with President Trump, as well as by voters specifically opposed to tariffs, by those trying to give national Democrats control of the Senate and by those prioritizing change over experience. A sizable 10% of voters say they could still change their minds — another dynamic that underscores that this could still break either way. Even when voters think Jackson's policies would make them financially better off, Collins gets almost one in five of those voters, too. Overall, Maine's voters do feel Trump's policies have hurt the Maine economy. Jackson wins most of those who do. But long-time service isn't entirely working against Collins, even if it's an "anti-incumbent" year: Collins does especially well among voters who say they've voted for her multiple times in the past. Jackson may be feeling the effects of the primary season: four in 10 Democrats and most independents wish someone else were the Democratic nominee. Jackson also runs behind the Democrats' gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree, as Pingree's lead in the governor's race hews much more closely to the state's overall partisan lean. (Kamala Harris won the state.) Pingree gets some of the voters who are splitting their tickets to back Collins. This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a representative sample of 1,144 registered voters in Maine interviewed between September 23rd -October 1, 2026. The sample was weighted according to gender, age, race and education based on  U.S. Census data, as well as to 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error is ± 4.7 points for registered voters. title: The Japanese V-Twin Engineered To Outlive Its Owner - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update A V-twin engine holds a very distinctive place in motorcycling history. American cruiser bikes are defined by their rumbling V-twin engines. The Ducati Panigale V2, the Aprilia RSV Mille, and the KTM RC8 are sportbikes that showcase the wild side of V-twin engines. Although more complex than a parallel-twin engine, V-twins (in existence since 1902) have shown notable refinement and durability. Who better to highlight these features than Japanese motorcycle makers, known for precision engineering? As a result, many Far East V-twin engines are designed to last much longer than their counterparts. The engine that interests us is a modern V-twin that has been around since 1983 and currently powers a timeless Honda cruiser bike. This is because Japanese motorcycle makers combine precision manufacturing tolerances, conservative engine tuning, and the philosophy of Kaizen (continuous refinement) in their engineering. The result is a relatively concise yet long-lasting lineup of V-twin-powered motorcycles. A V-twin engine is more adaptive than a comparable parallel-twin mill. They offer a narrower frontal profile, stronger low-end torque, and a lower center of gravity. This is why a V-twin engine works well on low-slung cruisers and nimble, urban-ready streetfighters. Beyond reliability, V-twins also add drama with a distinctive sound and visually pleasing design. Japanese V-twin engines, especially the long-standing ones, offer a balance of traditional and modern features that help them stay relevant for longer. Most V-twin engines in the Japanese portfolio are 20-plus years old and from Suzuki. The Boulevard C50 V-twin is 25 years old, the SV650 V-twin is 27 years old, and the mighty M109R power cruiser's V-twin is 20 years old. Interestingly, the youngest V-twin Japanese cruiser bike engine is the Yamaha Bolt R-Spec's 13-year-old 942 cc air-cooled mill. These long-lasting engines have stayed relevant for so long thanks to the manufacturer's formula of subtly updating them over the years with the necessary components. The most common upgrade is swapping carburetors for fuel injection. This adds a much-needed refresh without hampering reliability or refinement. Among the timeless bunch, the Honda Shadow Phantom stands out because its V-twin engine is a core design that is over 40 years old and has yet to show its age. The Honda Shadow V-twin engine's origin story dates back to the 1980s. Honda launched the 1983 VT750C with a liquid-cooled 45-degree SOHC V-twin. It had a displacement of roughly 749 cc, three valves per cylinder, and a six-speed manual gearbox with a final shaft drive. Then, due to US import tariffs imposed in 1984 on motorcycles over 701 cc, Honda temporarily downsized this engine to 700 cc on the VT700C. The next evolution came in 1998 with the return of the 750 cc V-twin on the Shadow ACE. Honda also changed the V-twin angle to 52 degrees for better balance. This engine has soldiered on without any major updates to date. The 750 cc V-twin is based on the 600 cc Shadow VLX 52-degree mill and was enlarged to 750 cc by increasing the bore by 4 mm and the stroke by 10 mm. Reliability is well catered for here with a simple engineering design featuring a SOHC layout, three valves per cylinder, and a low compression ratio. Add a low-stress performance tune to the mix, and we have an engine that can virtually go on forever with timely maintenance and preventive care. Honda also helps keep this mill relevant to 2026 standards with fuel injection that boosts refinement and helps meet modern emission standards. The latest iteration of this 745 cc liquid-cooled V-twin produces 44.9 horsepower at 5,500 RPM and 47.9 pound-feet of torque at 3,500 RPM. It has a 9.6:1 compression ratio, and the power curve is linear yet meaty at the lower end. Power goes to the rear wheel through a five-speed manual gearbox and a final shaft drive system. The Honda Shadow Phantom may be among the most dependable cruisers in the market today, but nothing is perfect, and neither is the Shadow Phantom. This Honda cruiser has been around for a long time, however, so Honda has ironed out most of the issues over the years. Some owners do report rare, relatively minor problems, so that most owners wouldn’t experience them. The most common such issue that owners report is related to the charging system. Like many older-generation Japanese cruisers, the Shadow Phantom’s stators and regulator can sometimes fail or wear out if subjected to heavy electrical loads. Some riders also report that the gearbox can feel a little clunky, especially when finding neutral. However, timely oil changes and drive shaft lubrication should keep this issue at bay. In high-mileage examples, some owners report minor oil weeping, too. Apart from these niggles, most owners say they don’t face any issues with the Shadow Phantom. It’s also worth keeping in mind that this bike has some limitations, including low passing power on the highway, a lack of low-end grunt due to the engine's inherent tuning, and a poor power-to-weight ratio. Still, for what this bike is worth, it remains one of the best value-for-money cruisers out there, and it will last for years to come with just routine maintenance. The same can’t be said for most of its rivals. The Shadow Phantom doesn't look outdated in 2026 because of its custom touches. This ten-year-old design still looks sharp thanks to blacked-out elements on almost every component. Honda seems to have taken a lot of inspiration from the 1950s Indian Chief. Notable cues include the low-slung, muscular design, a minimal headlamp enclosure, and the padded, scooped solo seat. Its dual-tone paint job on the teardrop fuel tank adds more visual drama. It also gets bobber-inspired chopped fenders that give those chunky tires a more dynamic presence. This design approach also helps the Shadow Phantom age better than its rivals. Its closest counterpart is the cool-looking Kawasaki Vulcan 900 Custom that fuses chopper styling with Japanese longevity. It also has a larger, long-standing 903 cc V-twin and cuts an attractive figure. But the Vulcan 900 is larger and heavier, making it better suited to the highway. The Shadow Phantom edges ahead for urban duties. Also, the Kawasaki costs more at $9,999. Then there's the Suzuki Boulevard C50, which leans more towards the classic side with lots of chrome and full-sized fenders. However, it's a bit too traditional, and features like pulled-back handlebars and floorboards make it more comfortable on highways only. While the Boulevard C50 is priced the same as the Honda Shadow Phantom ($9,299), it falls behind because Suzuki discontinued it for 2026. Despite staying true to the quintessential low-slung, stretched-out cruiser stance, the Honda Shadow Phantom is still relatively compact. It has a 64.5-inch wheelbase and a low seat height of 25.6 inches. The low seat height and five-inch ground clearance lower the center of gravity, aiding stability. The rider sits low and relaxed, with slightly forward-set footpegs and tall, wide handlebars. It also weighs a manageable 553 pounds, making it a comfortable daily runabout. The seat is well-scooped and padded to support long rides. Sturdy and proven underpinnings complement its near-immortal V-twin. The Shadow Phantom sits on a simple double-cradle steel frame that cocoons the V-twin. It is suspended by 41 mm forks up front with 5.5 inches of travel. The rear gets preload-adjustable twin shocks with 3.5 inches of travel. Braking is handled by a 296 mm disc coupled to a two-piston caliper up front. The rear gets a 276 mm disc coupled to a single-piston caliper. Fairly chunky 120/80 front and 160/80 rear tires, mounted on 17-inch front and 15-inch rear laced wheels, help the bike handle highway speeds and winding roads with confidence. There are no complex electronics here. This not only helps the Shadow Phantom stay timeless but also helps it be a comfortable first motorcycle for newbies. The onboard features are very basic, with the only notable feature being dual-channel ABS. Its instrument cluster is as simple as it gets: a large analog speedometer with a tiny bottom-mounted LCD to display data, including trip details. The absence of TFT screens and extensive driver-assist features keeps the overall build simple, too. This makes it easier and more affordable to repair. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. I have noticed there seems to always be some prejudice in your reviews. I own a 1998 Kawasaki Vulcan 1500 classic with over 100,000 miles and still see many on the road but have never seen any mention in your reviews. Aside from normal maintenence  these bikes are well built  and will last with just normal maintenence. title: What Thomson Reuters v. Ross Does and Doesn’t Say NOW About Fair Use and Generative AI - JDSupra
content:
In February 2025, I assessed the operative summary judgment opinion in Thomson Reuters v. Ross and guessed at what it might mean for generative AI copyright litigation. I drew a distinction between the “small model” AI at issue in Ross and the large language models (LLMs) at issue in many of the generative AI copyright litigations. I conjectured that the decision would be instructive, but not determinative, in the generative AI cases. A lot has happened since then. We have two subsequent decisions, Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta, that found that the use of content to train LLMs is allowed under the fair use doctrine. And now the Third Circuit has affirmed that February 2025 opinion in Ross, adopting some aspects of Judge Stephanos Bibas’ opinion but rejecting others. Although the opinion attempted to distinguish the LLM cases, the analytical framework deployed in the opinion might impact future generative AI cases. In doing so, the Third Circuit has diverged from Bartz v. Anthropic, setting up a possible circuit split. The opinion noted that “ROSS’s AI was not a generative AI, meaning it would not create any new expression; it would only return text passages from preexisting judicial opinions.” On this basis, the opinion dismissed concerns raised by the Department of Justice (DOJ) in another copyright AI fair use case, In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, over restrictive fair use opinions and their impact on American competition in the artificial intelligence industry. The opinion further minimized the DOJ’s concerns by noting that LLM training may not result in “substitutive competition” with the works that they are trained on, while ROSS’s AI training was for the express purpose of competing with Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw product. Thus, on the face of it, the opinion has limited applicability and ought not to have any impact on the LLM and other generative AI training cases. But the closer you look at the reasoning of the opinion, the more potentially impactful it becomes. The ROSS product was “an AI legal search engine that would respond to plain-language legal questions with relevant passages of text from judicial opinions.” To enable that search, the AI model “had to learn what made a judicial opinion responsive to a user’s legal question.” In other words, the “ROSS AI program [sought] to identify patterns regarding which judicial opinion passages respond well to legal questions.” To do that, ROSS used a vendor to create legal memos that in some instances contained Westlaw headnotes, and it used the headnotes to benchmark and rank responses to legal queries. There was no evidence that the ROSS program ever outputted Westlaw headnotes or that the Westlaw headnotes were used after the AI model was trained. Although the ROSS training was aimed at the noncopyrightable aspects of the Westlaw headnotes (i.e., detecting patterns of answer accuracy), the opinion nonetheless found the use was only minimally transformative: “ROSS’s platform uses Thomson Reuter’s headnotes to help users find judicial opinions related to their legal research inquiries, something Thomson Reuters already does with its headnotes.” At a certain degree of generality (i.e., if you zoom out far enough), that makes some sense. It is true that the ROSS product as a whole (which used other answer-accuracy benchmarks, software development techniques and source code) generally competes with Westlaw as a whole (which contains other headnotes besides the ones used as well as other software features and types of content). But there is a difference between nontransformative substitutive use and commercial competition. As Judge William Alsup noted in Bartz, “The Act seeks to advance original works of authorship, not to protect authors against competition.” Thus, the substitutive use must be aimed at the work itself (i.e., the headnotes used). This distinction was aptly articulated by Bibas in his 2023 summary judgment opinion: “[I]f Ross’s AI only studied the language patterns in the headnotes to learn how to produce judicial opinion quotes,” then ROSS’s use was transformative. If, however, ROSS’s use was “to get its AI to replicate and reproduce the creative drafting done by Westlaw’s attorney-editors,” then the use was not transformative. This distinction was lost in the subsequent 2025 summary judgment opinion and was not addressed at all in the Third Circuit opinion. Where the opinion stands to cause the most problems in future AI cases, however, is its application of a “strict” necessity standard to justify use of the underlying work. The opinion addressed the applicability of intermediate copying cases, in which software was downloaded to access noncopyrightable aspects of the software. The justification for copying in those cases was that there was no other way to access the nonprotectable aspects of the software but through the protectable code. The opinion converts the factual background of those intermediate copying cases into an immutable maxim: “Here, ROSS does not need to copy Thomson Reuters’s headnotes to access the underlying unprotected information. … It chose not to do so because copying the headnotes offered an ‘easy’ way to create its training memos. Unlike necessity, ease is not a justification for copying.” However, the standard for justifying use of the underlying work is not one of “strict necessity.” Under Warhol, the defendant need only show that the use was “reasonably necessary.” This distinction played an important role in Bartz, where the author plaintiffs argued that Anthropic did not strictly need to copy their specific books, or any books at all, to create its LLM. However, Anthropic demonstrated that there was a technological justification for the copying (i.e., the need to train on a “monumental” volume of texts), leading Alsup to conclude: “Because using so many works was reasonably necessary, using any one work for actually training LLMs was about as reasonable as the next.” Where does one draw the line then between “ease” and “reasonable necessity”? What cost threshold did ROSS have to cross before using the Westlaw headnotes was easy versus necessary? What technological challenges had to be posed? We don’t know, because the opinion doesn’t say. All eyes are currently on the generative AI copyright cases – 145 of them as of the date of this post. Those cases mostly involve LLMs or other multipurpose foundation models. But there is a great surge in enterprise use of AI to create fine-tuned or other “small models.” Those models might involve the use of content from competitors to obtain noncopyrightable information – market trends, competitive intelligence, product design ideas. If future courts interpret this opinion as prohibiting competitive uses and imposing a strict necessity standard, the impact it could have on the development of customized AI models is significant. title: Read the Bold Print: What Palazzo v. Bayview Means for Bankruptcy Disclaimers - Ward and Smith, P.A.
content:
Once a debtor files a bankruptcy petition, the stay kicks in and collection activity must grind to a halt to avoid exposing the creditor to liability. While the automatic stay prohibits creditors from attempting to collect on a debt, the stay does not eliminate the need to communicate altogether. Creditors typically still need to send certain account statements or provide other pertinent documents to a debtor about their account. But what should the creditor do when certain notifications may be in direct contravention of the automatic stay of the Bankruptcy Code? The Fourth Circuit’s recent decision in Palazzo v. Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC, provides welcome clarity. The court held that sending certain statements and communications will not violate the automatic stay, provided the appropriate disclaimers are included. Ruben Palazzo filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition in February 2016, to reorganize his debts. During his bankruptcy, his mortgage servicers continued sending him monthly account statements and 1098 tax forms, along with payoff statements that Palazzo had personally requested. Palazzo sued, alleging that those communications were efforts to collect on a debt which are prohibited by the automatic stay and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA). The district court ultimately sided with the mortgage servicer, which was upheld on appeal. The Court scrutinized the specific language in each of the communications. The Monthly Statements and Payoff Statements each provided a breakdown of the outstanding balance, the current interest rate, and other fees and amounts that would become due after the bankruptcy concluded. Critically, each statement included a prominent bankruptcy disclaimer that expressly notified the debtor that the statement was being sent “for informational and compliance purposes only” and that they were “not an attempt to collect a debt against [the debtor].” The Court found that the disclaimers were “clear and unequivocal,” and that a reasonable reader in Palazzo’s position would have understood that no payment was being demanded.  More importantly, Palazzo himself had requested the payoff statements, which undercut his argument that they were sent as an attempt to collect on a debt, rather than a ministerial response to his inquiry. The 1098 tax statements similarly contained information about the interest paid and remaining principal for tax purposes. While those statements did not contain any specific disclaimers, the Court held that they were clearly being sent to provide information to a debtor, necessary for him to complete his taxes. Because of that, the Court found that providing those forms did not evidence an intent to collect. The Palazzo decision confirms what careful creditors have long practiced, and it offers a blueprint for anyone who needs to communicate with a bankrupt debtor. Should a debtor allege a stay violation based on routine correspondence, the Palazzo framework provides a strong defense—so long as your communications contained proper disclaimers and did not demand payment. But be careful not to become complacent and treat all communications similarly. As noted, the Court paid particular attention to the exact wording of the disclaimers provided, and the facts surrounding those communications. As a result, careful drafting of form communications and periodic review of disclaimer language is important to ensure that there is no inadvertent violation of the automatic stay. Consult your attorney before sending notices to debtors who are in a pending bankruptcy proceeding or have received a discharge. ©

title: Doe v. State of Kansas - American Civil Liberties Union
content: Two transgender residents of Kansas filed a lawsuit in state court challenging SB 244, a state law enacted in 2026 that immediately invalidated the driver’s licenses of transgender people across the state and which authorizes anyone to sue anybody they suspect of being transgender for using the “wrong” restroom in government buildings. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. In early 2026, the Kansas state legislature passed SB 244, a law which prohibits transgender people from using public restrooms on government property that align with their gender identity and establishes a private right of action that allows anyone who suspects someone is transgender and in violation of the law to sue that person for “damages” totaling $1,000. The law also invalidates state-issued driver’s licenses with updated gender markers that reflect the carrier’s gender identity. In February 2026, transgender people across the state received letters from the state Department of Revenue’s Division of Vehicles informing them that their driver’s licenses “will no longer be valid,” effective immediately. SB 244 also prohibits transgender Kansans – or those born in Kansas - from updating the gender marker on state-issued birth certificates and driver’s licenses in the future. The same day SB 244 went into effect, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Kansas, and Ballard Spahr LLP filed a lawsuit challenging SB 244 in the District Court of Douglas County on behalf of two transgender men who had their driver’s licenses invalidated under the law. The lawsuit charges that SB 244 violates the Kansas Constitution’s protections for personal autonomy, privacy, equality under the law, due process, and freedom of speech. “The invalidation of state-issued IDs threatens to out transgender people against their will every time they apply for a job, rent an apartment, or interact with police,” said Harper Seldin, Senior Staff Attorney for the ACLU’s LGBTQ & HIV Rights Project. “Taken as a whole, SB 244 is a transparent attempt to deny transgender people autonomy over their own identities and push them out of public life altogether.” Click here to learn more about SB 244 and what it means for transgender people. If you or a loved one is impacted by Senate Bill 244 becoming a law, contact us by visiting aclu.org/KS_SB244. We want to hear from you. Update: A hearing on the motion for a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of SB 244 has been scheduled for September 29, 2026.
